paragraphs: Twenty seconds. That was the whole act, and the snails had come a very long way to see it. They filled the greenhouse in rows, on flowerpots and fogged glass, each pointing two soft eye-stalks at the stage, which was a seed tray. A clock on the wall began to count down. Yellow Duck Sweater stepped onto the damp soil and felt it give under its orange feet. It sat. It stood. It tilted its head. The snails did nothing at all, and the duck began to worry, because how did a snail vote? Then rain ticked on the roof, and in the back row one snail slowly began to leave.

It was not leaving. It was coming forward, one shiny centimetre at a time, and behind it came the rest. A snail, the duck understood, votes by arriving. So it sang its little song, then sang it slower, then slower still, stretching each note to the speed of the audience. Three copies of itself stepped out from behind a flowerpot, the way copies do in the simulator, and joined in on the wheee. By the time the last snail touched the seed tray, the floor was crossed with silver trails, every one pointing at four small ducks in the lamplight, and the clock had politely stopped at one.

imagePrompt: Yellow Duck Sweater, a small two-legged tabletop robot. Its head is a smooth, chunky white plastic shell shaped like a small loaf of bread: about one and a half times as long front to back as it is tall, deep and boxy with softly rounded corners and a mostly flat top. It is not a round dome or ball, and not a long thin tube. It has an orange trim along the bottom edge and a small orange hinge on each side. At the front of the head is a single round camera eye: a black lens inside a thick orange-yellow ring. It has no beak and no mouth. The head sits on a tall, thin neck, about as tall as the head is long, made of stacked black servo motors with a few loose black wires, leaning slightly forward. Its body is a small, boxy white torso with rounded corners. It has no arms and no hands. Its short legs are black servo joints with white plastic covers on the hips, knees slightly bent. Its feet are flat and rounded like duck feet, orange on top with yellow soles. It wears a small, chunky-knit, bright lemon-yellow crewneck sweater over its white torso, slightly too big, with a ribbed collar, cuffs, and hem. Knitted into the front of the sweater is a simple cartoon duckling: pale yellow body with a thick black outline, a black dot eye, a curved line for its wing, an orange beak, and orange feet. A single full-color comic page with six panels of equal size in a grid of two columns and three rows, separated by clean white gutters, read left to right and top to bottom. The same robot duck appears in every panel and looks identical each time, unless a panel says otherwise. No speech bubbles, captions, sound effects, panel numbers, or any other text. Panel 1: Inside a cozy greenhouse at night, the robot duck in its yellow duckling sweater stands on a seed tray used as a small stage, while rows of snails sit on flowerpots and along the misty glass walls, all pointing their eye-stalks at it, and a round wall clock hangs above. Panel 2: On the seed tray stage the duck sits down on the damp soil with its orange feet sticking out, head tilted, while the snails in the audience stay perfectly still. Panel 3: Rain streaks the greenhouse roof as the duck looks nervously toward the back row, where one snail has turned and started to crawl. Panel 4: Close-up of the floor: the snail is crawling toward the stage, not away, leaving a shiny silver trail, with many more snails following behind it. Panel 5: Four ducks stand side by side on the seed tray, the yellow-sweater duck plus three identical copies in matching yellow duckling sweaters stepping out from behind a flowerpot, all with heads raised as if singing. Panel 6: Seen from above, the greenhouse floor is crossed by dozens of glowing silver snail trails that all lead to the seed tray, where four ducks in yellow sweaters stand in warm lamplight surrounded by snails, the wall clock above them. Warm children's comic art: clean confident ink outlines, soft flat colors with gentle shading, a dreamy night palette, cozy and a little surreal. Friendly for an 11-year-old. No text, letters, logos, or numbers anywhere in the image. Real people do not appear.
